conversation.content:
Hello—thank you for making time for this visit. My name is Sarah; I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. Over the next few minutes we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS for short). It’s a brief, well-studied set of ten questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past week of new motherhood. Everything you share is confidential; if any answer suggests a safety concern we’ll talk through supports together, but otherwise our conversation stays private between you and your care team. I’ll re-phrase each item in everyday language, and you can answer however feels most comfortable—there are no right or wrong responses. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve still been able to laugh sometimes—like when the baby made those silly faces during tummy-time—but it definitely feels harder than before. I have to remind myself to lighten up, and a lot of jokes just fall flat for me lately.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes, but it’s definitely taken more effort than usual. Most of the time I’ve had to fake it or I just don’t find things as funny as I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to some things—like when my mom comes over to hold the baby so I can take a shower—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. It feels more like I’m just getting through the day than actually enjoying much.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week. Like when he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. and I kept thinking maybe I’m just not doing something right, or I must’ve eaten something that bothered him. Rationally I know babies just cry, but the “it’s my fault” thought still pops in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A few nights I’ve lain awake with my heart racing, running through all the “what-ifs” about the baby—like whether he’s breathing okay or if that tiny cough means something awful. Nothing specific happened to set it off; it just shows up and I can’t shut it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—just that rush of worry I told you about. I haven’t had a full-on panic spell, but I do get this sudden knot in my stomach when I imagine something bad happening to him, even when everything looks fine.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… a few days this week it felt like the feedings, the laundry, the constant holding—everything—just piled up. I’m managing, but I end those days exhausted and thinking “I can’t do one more thing,” even though I know I’ll still have to.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not every night—maybe three or four times this week—but I do lie there replaying the day, worrying I missed something or that tomorrow will be harder, and then I can’t drift off even when the baby’s out cold.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve had moments—usually toward evening—where I just feel kind of heavy and teary, like the sadness sits on my chest for a while. It’s not all day, but it keeps popping up, and I can’t always shake it off.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t actually cried much—maybe once or twice when I was especially worn out. I feel like I could cry more often, but I hold it back because I’m scared once I start I won’t be able to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I want to be here for my baby—I just want to feel better so I can enjoy him instead of feeling so drained all the time.

Hearing how hard you're trying to laugh and look forward to things, yet feeling that heavy, teary weight each evening, tells me you're carrying much more than the usual new-mum load. You described pushing through the days, second-guessing yourself at 3 a.m., and lying awake with racing worries even when your baby is peacefully asleep. These feelings are common, but they're also signals that you deserve extra support right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment requiring effort to laugh, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports noticeably diminished enjoyment and anticipation, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "a couple of times this week" and gives examples, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, unprovoked anxiety episodes that are hard to control, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes periodic overwhelm and exhaustion but still managing, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports 3–4 nights of sleep difficulty linked to unhappiness and worry, fitting "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring, noticeable sadness that intrudes multiple times and lingers, best matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: anhedonia (Q1-2), inappropriate guilt (Q3), psychomotor agitation/anxiety (Q4-5), fatigue and feeling overwhelmed (Q6-8), and mood-related insomnia (Q7). Scoring 17 falls well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable depression, while Q10 = 0 shows no current self-harm risk. Combined with functional impairment (<quote>I'm just getting through the day</quote>), these findings warrant urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> or <med>PCP</med>
2. Begin daily mood charting; note sleep, anxiety spikes, and enjoyment levels
3. Schedule brief supportive counselling sessions while waiting for specialist review
4. Share results with partner/family and create a list of practical help they can give
5. Practice 10-minute wind-down routine before bed to reduce nighttime worry
6. Allow yourself permission to set small daily goals rather than tackling everything
7. Keep all follow-up appointments even if you start feeling better
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant approx. ≤ 3 mo) – self-report

Primary endorsed symptoms  
- Persistent low mood, “heavy and teary,” worse evenings  
- Marked loss of pleasure/interest (anhedonia); laughter feels effortful or forced  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame re infant care (middle-of-night crying spells)  
- Recurrent intrusive “what-ifs,” racing heart, nocturnal worry → difficulty initiating sleep even when infant asleep  
- Feeling overwhelmed; several days “can’t do one more thing”  
- Sub-threshold crying spells (suppressed)  
- No self-harm ideation; explicitly denies (protective factor)

Patterns / risk indicators  
- Meets sub-threshold to threshold criteria for depressive symptoms (mood, anhedonia, guilt, sleep disturbance)  
- Co-occurring anxiety symptoms (GAD-like worry, somatic arousal)  
- Functional impact: sleep deprivation, fatigue, diminished confidence in parenting  
- No psychosis, no suicidal/homicidal thoughts reported

Screening impression  
Elevated risk for postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; scores would likely fall within moderate range on standardized tools (e.g., EPDS ≥ 10–12). No immediate safety concerns. Recommend formal assessment (EPDS/PHQ-9/GAD-7), psychoeducation, supportive counseling, and consideration of referral to perinatal mental health specialist for further evaluation and stepped care planning.

End of screening note
